Sigh. Game journalist here.

I suspected that GameLoading wasn't any good when their PR person told me to buy a copy.

Frankly, I disagree with what a lot of this guy is saying regarding games and politics- I think people should be free to add their own opinions of all sorts to games. Nobody's going to force him to play- or even agree. I don't think that a documentary about the culture around indie games is under any obligation to talk about mechanics, as this guy says they should.

"A lot of these tiny pixel graphics aren't even made by artists."

This guy just keeps ragging on games that he doesn't like, and it's as though he's more interested in tearing people and their work down than providing honest criticism of GameLoading. Both he- and the awful movie he's supposed to be criticizing- are very clearly biased.

And for the record, Quinn did get a lot of abuse prior to GG- I remember when Depression Quest was on Steam Greenlight, a bunch of folks were sending nasty tweets; you can verify if somebody is being harassed on Twitter simply by searching for tweets containing their handle.

I think that there's room in games for everybody- games for pink-haired hipsters who want to talk about social issues and games for people who actually care about, you know... Games.

Regarding the IGF, what I've heard about it really has my attention- what's the criteria for games to win? Who are the judges? Where's the transparency?

But speaking as a game journalist, I can honestly say that success is not dependent on being part of an indie clique. If you make a game that interests a group of people, there will be people willing to buy, and there will be a community ready to play. Look at the success of Robot Roller Derby Disco Dodgeball- the developer of that game is one of the quietest I know, and yet he's seen success. Last time I checked he wasn't affiliated with any particular clique.
